problem: Robots rarely exploit real-world navigational signs for mapless navigation. Prior sign-based methods (e.g. ReasonNav) handle only simple 4-cardinal-direction signs, rely on a single partial view or a global map, and use geometry-only path detection, so they fail on complex, diverse signage and outdoor scenes.
motivation: Humans navigate unfamiliar buildings via signs without maps, but interpreting a sign requires common sense, parsing of complex symbols, and a coherent model of the partially observed local 3D scene. VLMs have the needed semantics but are sensitive to how spatial information is represented, so the paper looks for a representation VLMs can reason over.
key_idea: Build a sign-centric, sign-aligned, simplified 2D top-down abstract map (SignScene) of the local scene with labeled boxes and lettered path frontiers, and have a VLM ground the sign instruction as a multiple-choice selection over it.
insight: Representation matters more than the foundation model: ReasonNav also uses foundation models but gets 30/114 against 101/114 for SignScene, which the authors attribute to sign-centric framing, exploration, semantic path segmentation and general sign parsing (these factors are argued, not individually ablated on grounding). The parsing ablation shows in-context symbol prototypes (53→61/114) and temporal fusion of multiple observations (61→93/114) both matter a lot.
method: SignScene structure: tuple (S, R_obj, R_dir) of signs, navigational structures (escalator, lift, stairs) and traversable regions, rendered as a simplified 2D top-view map centred on and oriented with the sign's pose

3D map construction: monocular depth (Metric3Dv2) plus odometry; signs detected with GroundingDINO, segmented with SAM2 and clustered over time by centroid and normal; structures fused via Hungarian matching; traversable area segmented with GeNIE

Sign understanding: VLM parses sign image into (location, instruction) pairs using an in-context symbol dictionary of prototypes, extended to stairs/escalators/compound directions; cues merged across frames by majority vote

Rendering: the traversable-area contour is simplified to a polygon; candidate path points are placed at convex protrusions and labeled with letters, and structures are drawn as labeled oriented boxes, giving a multiple-choice problem
Active perception: detect a sign, visually servo (and move the Spot arm) to view it head-on, rotate in place to find frontiers, then visit frontiers sequentially to complete the local map

Reasoning: fuzzy Levenshtein matching of the goal against parsed locations across signs; the VLM (GPT-5) picks the lettered path or object closest to the goal and consistent with its instruction; the choice is converted to a 3D subgoal, and for the benchmark the nearest of 4 answers is selected

setting.backbone: GPT-5 (frozen) for grounding; Gemini-2.5-Pro for sign understanding in the online system; GroundingDINO, SAM2, GeNIE, Metric3Dv2 as frozen perception modules
setting.training_data: none (training-free; uses pretrained foundation models and a small sign symbol dictionary for in-context learning)
setting.observation: monocular RGB (hand-held/Spot camera) with visual-inertial odometry; depth inferred by monocular estimator
setting.action_space: SE(2) subgoal selected from candidate frontiers/objects (benchmark: 4-way multiple choice)
setting.simulator: real world only (offline hand-held recordings plus Spot robot)
setting.privileged: none (benchmark ground-truth answers used only for scoring; ground truth sign parsing used only in ablation scoring)

numbers_note: The benchmark is the authors' own, not a standard one; the baseline ReasonNav gets 30/114. The real-world demo is qualitative with no success rate.
results: On the authors' 114-query, 9-environment grounding benchmark, SignScene reaches 101/114 (88.6%), against 30/114 for ReasonNav. Sign parsing improves from 38/114 (Agrawal et al.) and 53/114 (ReasonNav-style prompt) to 93/114 with in-context learning and temporal fusion. A Spot robot completed a mapless navigation demo to 'TERRACE' using signs only.
limitations: Depends on open-set detector quality (false positives/negatives for escalators, etc.), and traversability maps are incomplete in crowded areas
Compound and context-dependent signs are still parsed poorly, and the VLM can still fail on instructions like 'left-then-forward' or be misled by text such as 'exit c'

Evaluation is on a small self-collected benchmark against one baseline, the real-world demo is a single qualitative example, and VLM queries are slow (GPT-5 grounding takes about 20 s), with no full navigation pipeline
